---
title: "Simple simulation: two Gaussians"
subtitle: "Two 2-D Gaussians oscillating in phase at the same frequency — what separates them, and where that information ends up"
---

Second controlled object, one step closer to a real B-scan: **two** 2-D
Gaussians in the same image, oscillating vertically at the same frequency and
in phase. No noise at all — the question here is the exact structure of the
decomposition, not its robustness, which
[Simple simulation: one Gaussian](svd-simple-simulation.qmd) already covers.

The question this answers: **does the SVD give one component per oscillator, or
one per motion?** Two synchronous oscillators share a single time signal
$s(t)$, so the first-order term of the displacement,
$A(x)\,s(t)\,\partial I/\partial y$, is rank 1 — one component for both, with
whatever distinguishes them folded into the *spatial* vector $u_1$ and gone
from the *temporal* vector $v_1$. That matters directly for the choroid, where
every A-scan pulsates on the same cardiac cycle: no $v_k$ will ever separate
them.

Three experiments, each changing **exactly one** property between the two
Gaussians, so that what lands in $u_1$ can be attributed without ambiguity:

| | what differs | left | right |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | motion amplitude | 8 px | 2 px |
| 2 | intensity | 1.00 | 0.50 |
| 3 | standard deviation | 7 px | 3.5 px |

Taken together they show that $u_1$ does **not** weigh amplitude — it weighs
amplitude × intensity, and is indifferent to size. Twenty singular vectors are
shown in each case, far past the useful rank, so that the two places where the
decomposition stops describing the simulation — spectral folding above Nyquist,
then the floating-point floor — are visible rather than assumed.

Each experiment also runs the **two phase estimators** that
`Astronauts/compute_one_cycle_compare_methods.py` puts head to head on the real
cohort — the FIR band-pass (`1_fir`) and multichannel SSA (`3a_mssa`) — against
a phase that is here *known analytically* rather than estimated. On real data
neither can be checked against a ground truth; here both can.
